title: DNA Nanotubes as a Versatile Tool to Study Semiflexible Polymers
protocol: Purchase DNA sequences from a suitable DNA synthesis service.
Resuspend lyophilized oligonucleotides in purified water.
Follow resuspension steps given in the corresponding manual from the company.
Adjust the amount of water to obtain a final concentration of 200 µM.
Determine concentrations of the single DNA strands via UV-Vis spectroscopy at 260 nm.
Calculate the concentration of the oligonucleotides using extinction coefficients for each sequence.
Mix DNA strands-each at the same concentration-in a container suitable for the thermocycler to form desired nHTs.
Ensure final buffer conditions are 1xTE and 12.5 mM MgCl2.
Hybridize the nHTs in a thermocycler by denaturing for 10 min at 90 °C, followed by a quick drop to 65 °C.
Decrease temperature slowly from 65 °C to 55 °C with complementary base pairing over 20 steps of -0.5 K each for 30 min.
Quickly decrease temperature from 55 °C to 20 °C after the slow decrease steps.
Store hybridized nHTs at 4 °C for up to 3 weeks without detectable degradation.
For fluorescence microscopy, partially substitute U1 with modified U1-Cy3 during hybridization.
Dilute the sample to the desired final concentration using the sample buffer.
Choose an appropriate geometry for the dynamic shear rheometer based on the sample volume.
Load the sample onto the dynamic shear rheometer.
Surround the sample with 2.5 mL of the sample buffer bath.
Add a surfactant just below the micelle concentration around the sample.
Use a Hamilton syringe to surround the sample with lipid to avoid air contact.
Seal the sample chamber with a cap equipped with wet sponges.
If possible, add an additional water bath outside the sample chamber to further suppress evaporation.
Start the measurement using rheometer-specific software at room temperature.
Alternatively, perform the measurement at 37 °C if physiological conditions are required.
Allow the sample to equilibrate for 2 hours at room temperature.
Perform a short f-sweep (e.g., strain γ = 5%, frequency f = 0.01 Hz to 30 Hz, 5 data points per decade).
Perform a long f-sweep (e.g., strain γ = 5%, frequency f = 0.001 Hz to 30 Hz, 21 data points per decade); optionally omit the low-frequency regime to reduce measurement time.
Perform another short f-sweep.
Perform a γ-sweep (e.g., frequency f = 1 Hz, strain γ = 0.0125% to 100%, 20 data points per decade).
Prepare 8 aliquots of 12 μL for each sample using 1-4 μM DNA per strand, 12.5 mM MgCl2 in 1x TE buffer, and 1x nucleic acid gel stain from a 10,000x DMSO stock.
Make a negative control with no DNA but include nucleic acid gel stain.
Transfer the aliquots to a real-time PCR plate and seal with adhesive film.
Centrifuge the plate at 100 x g for 1 min at room temperature to remove gas bubbles.
Load the sealed plate into a real-time quantitative PCR system.
Run an annealing program.
Denature the DNA at 90 °C for 10 min.
Drop the temperature quickly to 72 °C.
Decrease the temperature slowly by 0.5 °C every 30 min.
Accelerate the temperature ramp after the signal has decayed.
Ensure the lid of the cycler heats to at least 100°C to prevent condensation on the adhesive film during PCR amplification.
Excite samples with an argon-ion laser at 488 nm and detect fluorescence at 550 nm when using nucleic acid gel stain or a spectrally similar dye.
Measure the fluorescence signal frequently to enhance overall quality, ideally every 9 seconds.
Subtract the previous mean value from the current mean value for each temperature step to obtain the relative change in fluorescent signal.
Use a cantilever tip with high stiffness.
Determine the resonance frequency of the cantilever using internal AFM software.
Record the height profile with the AFM in air.
Perform recording in tapping mode at low scan rates to avoid damaging or displacing the nHTs.
